excerpt: 1 Quantitative Journalism: Computer Assisted Reporting and Research ENL 327 · Augsburg College · Fall 2010 Wednesdays, 6-9 p.m., Foss 22B Instructor: Steve Aggergaard Office: Memorial 219B Work (Bassford Remele law firm): 612-376-1614 Cell phone: 651-402-8505 (OK to text me) Preferred email during the day: saggergaard@bassford.com Other addresses: aggergaa@augsburg.edu saggergaard@yahoo.com Required texts: Computer-Assisted Reporting, A Practical Guide by Brant Houston Associated Press Stylebook (or online version, iPhone app, or www.apstylebook.com) Other required reading: New York Times’ Economix blog: http://economix.blogs.nytimes.com/ The Uptake: www.theuptake.org Minnesota Public Radio Polinaut blog: http://minnesota.publicradio.org/collections/special/columns/polinaut/ New York Times’ The Caucus blog: http://thecaucus.blogs.nytimes.com Online Journalism Review: www.ojr.org Other articles as noted below and as the course and news develop … Course Description Welcome to “Quantitative Journalism: Computer Assisted Reporting and Research.” This is a reporting class. Computers will assist you to get you where you need to go, which will be off campus, in the community, our community, reporting the news. We have four scheduled opportunities to cover the news off-campus during the term—on Sept. 22, Sept. 29, Oct. 6, and Oct. 20. Each event is during our scheduled class time, so please plan accordingly. You’ll write stories from each of those events by reporting from the scene but also incorporating computer-assisted research you performed previously. If you are unable to attend the event, you will be expected to compensate by finding a similar off-campus event, personally attending it, and incorporating computer-assisted reporting to complete your story by deadline time. 2 Late submissions might or might not be submitted, depending on the circumstances, but will not be eligible for full credit. For the first few stories, rough drafts will be due to me by noon on the Monday before class. I will then critique your rough drafts and hand them back during class on Wednesday and final drafts will be due the following week. Your grade will be based on your stories, computer-assisted research assignments, and several quizzes on the assigned reading. About one-quarter of your grade will be based on a final project involving an off-campus subject of your choosing that includes both computer-assisted reporting and reporting from “people” sources. The parameters of the project are designed to be open- ended. We will work together so your final project is tailored to your interests and career goals. Working in teams not only will be allowed but will be encouraged. When an assignment calls for written piece of journalism, you may prepare either a “print”-type story suitable for a newspaper or news website, or a broadcast script suitable for radio, television, podcast, or online video. Your final project may be any combination of media and forms that you choose. Unless otherwise noted or arranged ahead of time, your audience for each piece of journalism will be a general Twin Cities audience. Extra credit: You may earn up to 10 points for each story (not part of the course or any employment) that you submit to news outlets including but not limited to the Echo. Please talk to me
